extracted.intended_audience: teachers, school boards, parents, school physicians/oculists, and public health officials concerned with children's eyesight
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and procedural recommendations for detecting, preventing, and limiting the development of near-sight (myopia) in schoolchildren through examinations, classroom/teaching practices, lighting, furniture, and hygiene measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic use of atropia to distinguish true myopia from spasm
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine absolutely whether the eyeball has taken the abnormal elongated shape (true myopia) or whether apparent near-sight is due to a spasmodic action of the muscle of accommodation, the oculist must paralyze that muscle by a weak solution of sulphate of atropia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When atropia cannot be applied, resort to the ophthalmoscope. Paralyzing accommodation allows object-tests and trial-glasses to determine the question with certainty. Examiner's accommodation must also be relaxed for full accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the ophthalmoscope when atropia is impracticable
rubrics_metrics.description: If it be impracticable to apply atropia, then the ophthalmoscope must be resorted to, as offering the nearest approach to certainty of results when the accommodating muscle cannot be paralyzed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiner holds a small mirror with a hole close to the patient's eye and inspects the illuminated interior; if the retina is not clearly visible (assuming no media opacity), anterior convergence (myopia) is indicated and a concave glass can be used to confirm degree.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object-tests and trial-glasses to determine degree of refractive error
rubrics_metrics.description: Object-tests and trial-glasses can recognize myopia or hypermetropia when the degree exceeds the adjustability of the lens; degree is indicated by the strength of the correcting glass.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use trial-glasses to interpose concave/convex lenses and observe correction; combine with ophthalmoscopic findings or atropia as needed for certainty.

rubrics_metrics.name: School-entry and periodic eyesight examinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Examinations of the sight of all children when they first enter school, and at such subsequent stages of their education as might seem desirable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination results can govern seat placement relative to blackboard and other classroom accommodations. Successive examinations will help determine improvement after adopting preventive means and furnish standards for comparing schools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of a permanent official examining oculist and provision of glasses
rubrics_metrics.description: Advocacy for a permanent official oculist who may recommend glasses in some cases, and that glasses, if necessary, should be furnished at public expense or from a special fund and worn at least during school hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Having a permanent examiner allows consistent screening and follow-up; providing glasses removes financial barriers to correction and classroom accommodation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach primary letter-forms from large models or blackboards rather than books
rubrics_metrics.description: Type and script letters and figures, and their primary combinations, at least, should never be taught from books, but from large and perfectly-formed models printed on cards and hung on the wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Train the eye and memory to recognize letters at sight before introducing small book forms to avoid early strain; use large models to reduce near-focus demand in early instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delay fine near work (books, slates, writing-paper) until eye/hand training achieved
rubrics_metrics.description: Too early use by school-children of books, slates, and writing-paper should be avoided; large free-hand drawing on good-sized slates should precede formation of letters and figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When beginning writing, make letters of generous size; prioritize correct position over fine work until posture becomes habitual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforce correct head/body/book position as imperative requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: A correct position should be an imperative requirement; until it becomes habitual and easy, good work should be of secondary importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent prone or forward head positions, reading with the book in the lap, and ensure desks are graded to pupil height. Distance from eye to page should be 12–18 inches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic inspection of writing materials and rules for acceptable materials
rubrics_metrics.description: Hard slate-pencils and greasy slate-surfaces should not be permitted; both should be subject to systematic inspection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure materials promote comfortable, non-straining writing and drawing; avoid substitutes (e.g., lead-pencil in evening) that increase strain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teacher/parent responsibility for preventing faulty positions and providing physiological instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Ignorance or laxity on the part of parents and primary teachers in permitting faulty positions of the head, body, and book during reading, study, and writing should be countered and early intelligent cooperation of the pupil secured by simple physiological instruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Active supervision, correction of posture, and short physiologic lessons for pupils to understand eye-care are recommended.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work-rest guideline: frequent rest and change of visual focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid prolonged and steady looking at near objects without rest or frequent change of the visual focus, as in long and absorbed novel-reading, intense study, or persistent needlework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At brief intervals rest the eyes by looking off and away from the book for a few moments; prevent continuous sustained accommodation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reading at too short range and ensure proper illumination/direction of light
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading or otherwise using the sight at too short range results in part from insufficient light, faulty direction of light causing shadows on the page, or direct rays falling upon the eye causing undue pupil contraction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure sufficient and properly directed light (in writing, light should be received over the left shoulder), avoid shadows cast by hand/body, and prevent direct glare on the eyes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Furniture and desk standards: graded desks and recommended desk geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Desks should be graded to the height of the pupil; the distance of the eye from the page should be 12–18 inches; the front of the desk should overlap the seat one or two inches. Desks set too far from seats induce faulty position.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donders favored high, sloping desks and warned against rectilinear drawing on flat surfaces. Proper desk design prevents stooping and forward head posture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vitiated (bad) air in the school-room
rubrics_metrics.description: A vitiated atmosphere is a frequent feature of the school-room and its effect is indirectly to injure, if not to destroy, the sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain ventilation and fresh air to preserve general and visual health; consider air quality as a contributing factor to eye strain and disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sun-glare and abrupt transitions of lighting
rubrics_metrics.description: Allowing a sun-glare on the page while reading, and transitions from cloud-shadow to sunshine, are harmful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent glare on reading surfaces and avoid seating or positioning that exposes pupils to changing direct sunlight which strains the eyes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reading/studying in railroad-cars and twilight-reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading and studying in railroad-cars is known to be a fruitful source of injury; twilight-reading (prolonging study after daylight declines) is especially pernicious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discourage reading in moving vehicles and avoid studying as daylight fades; do not rely on artificial illumination that is poor or improperly arranged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textbook caution: prefatory eye-care notice to readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Recommendation that a brief and appropriate caution be conspicuously printed in the front of every school and college text-book advising (1) sufficient light and correct angle (light over left shoulder in writing), (2) avoid stooping and hold the book up, sit erect when writing, (3) rest the eyes at brief intervals, and avoid small or poorly printed text and straining the sight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested wording: 'Reader, your eyesight is worth more to you than any information you are likely to gain from this book...' followed by the enumerated cautions. Also advise cleansing eyes with soft water morning and evening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition that myopia is generally incurable but preventable
rubrics_metrics.description: All authorities agree that it is incurable, and all agree that it may be prevented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes focus on prevention via school practices, examinations, accommodation, and hygiene rather than expecting cure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated principal causes and physiological rationale for development of near-sight
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal causes listed: (1) premature use of books/slates/writing-paper, (2) faulty positions/ignorance of parents/teachers, (3) prolonged steady near looking without rest, (4) using sight at too short range (insufficient/ faulty light, wrong desks, small type), (5) prone/forward head positions, (6) vitiated atmosphere, (7) sun-glare/transitions, (8) reading in railroad-cars, (9) insufficient light/twilight-reading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides physiological explanations: prolonged tension lessens muscular elasticity; inward-pulling muscles cause transverse protrusion/elongation of the eyeball; prone head position increases blood in eyes causing softening and distention. Use these mechanisms to justify preventive measures above.
